text: Theorem 2.2 (Accuracy-dependent query complexity lower bound) . Let $d\geq 3$ , $L,\Delta>0$ , $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $0<\delta<\frac{\Delta}{L},\qquad 0<\epsilon<\frac{L}{3}.$ For every integer $T\geq 1$ satisfying $T+1\leq\left(\frac{L-\epsilon}{2\epsilon}\right)^{(d-2)/2},$ (2.10) and every deterministic algorithm $A$ in the local-oracle model above, there exists a fixed $f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})$ with $\tau_{A}(f;\mathbf{x}_{0},\delta,\epsilon)>T$ . Every point actually queried among the first $T$ calls, and the output if $A$ returns within $T$ calls, satisfies $\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{q}))>\epsilon.$ Moreover, $f(\mathbf{x}_{0})=0$ , $\inf f=-\Delta$ , and $\mathrm{int}(\arg\min f)\neq\varnothing$ .

Theorem 2.3 (Deterministic zeroth-order query bound) . Let $d\geq 1$ , $L,\Delta,\delta>0$ , $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $0<\epsilon<L$ . A deterministic algorithm using only function values returns a $(\delta,\epsilon)$ -Goldstein stationary point of every $f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})$ within $1+\left(\frac{2\Delta}{\delta\epsilon}+1\right)\left(1+\frac{4L}{\epsilon}\right)^{d}$ (2.11) total calls. If $\epsilon\geq L$ , the initial point is already valid and the prescribed initial call suffices.

Corollary 2.4 (Fixed-accuracy exponential dimension dependence) . For every $d\geq 4$ and $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\left\lfloor\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^{(d-2)/2}\right\rfloor\leq\mathcal{T}_{\rm det}\left(d,1,1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{8};\mathbf{x}_{0}\right)\leq 1+33^{d+1}.$ Consequently, the fixed-accuracy complexity is $\exp(\Theta(d))$ . There is no uniform deterministic bound that is a joint polynomial in $(d,\delta^{-1},\epsilon^{-1})$ for the full function class, even with $L=\Delta=1$ .

Proposition 3.3 (Consistency with affine oracle responses) . Let $d\geq 3$ and $S=\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{q}_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a nonempty finite set of distinct points. Fix $0<\alpha<\gamma<1$ satisfying ( 3.1 ), choose $\beta>1/c_{\gamma}$ , and define $L_{F}$ by ( 3.6 ). Given $L,\Delta>0$ and $0<\delta<\Delta/L$ , there exist a fixed function $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ , a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ , and a common radius $\rho>0$ such that: (i) $\Lip(f)\leq L$ , $\inf f=-\Delta$ , and $\mathrm{int}(\arg\min f)\neq\varnothing$ ; (ii) for every $i$ and $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{B}_{\rho}^{\circ}(\mathbf{q}_{i})$ , $f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{L}{L_{F}}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{i}),\qquad\bigl(f(\mathbf{q}_{i}),\partial f(\mathbf{q}_{i})\bigr)=(0,\{L\mathbf{e}_{1}/L_{F}\});$ (3.14) (iii) for every $i$ and $\mathbf{g}\in\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{q}_{i})$ , $\left\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{u}\right\rangle=\frac{L\alpha}{L_{F}},$ (3.15) and consequently $\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{0},\partial_{\delta}f(\mathbf{q}_{i}))\geq\frac{L\alpha}{L_{F}}.$ (3.16) If $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in S$ , then $f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})$ , $f(\mathbf{x}_{0})=0$ , and its initial gap is exactly $\Delta$ .

Proposition 5.3 (Dimension-free first-order query bound) . Let $d\geq 1$ , $L,\Delta,\delta>0$ , $\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $L/\sqrt{2}<\epsilon<L$ . Algorithm 2 returns a $(\delta,\epsilon)$ -Goldstein stationary point of every $f\in\mathcal{F}_{d}(L,\Delta;\mathbf{x}_{0})$ within $2+\frac{\Delta L}{\delta(2\epsilon^{2}-L^{2})}$ (5.6) first-order oracle calls.

Proposition A.1 (Transfer to an algorithm-chosen initial point) . Consider a deterministic algorithm that chooses its initial point from $(d,L,\Delta,\delta,\epsilon)$ before seeing any oracle information, makes its first query there, and counts that call. A uniform $T$ -call guarantee under that convention induces a uniform $T$ -call guarantee in the fixed-initial-point model at the particular initial point it chooses. Consequently, Theorem 2.2 , which holds for every prescribed $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ , transfers to that convention without losing a query.

Proposition C.1 (The finite hard instance is DC) . Every finite hard instance produced by Proposition 3.3 is DC. If $N=1$ , then the construction is $F(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{1}),\qquad f(\mathbf{x})=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}_{1}),-\Delta\right\},$ and $f$ is convex. Taking $p=f$ and $q=0$ gives $\Lip(q)=0=L(N-1),\qquad\Lip(p)\leq L=LN.$ If $N\geq 2$ , let $F_{1},\ldots,F_{N}$ be the branches in ( 3.11 ), let $F=\min_{i}F_{i}$ , and define $H(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}F_{i}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad K(\mathbf{x})=\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\sum_{j\neq i}F_{j}(\mathbf{x}).$ Then $H$ and $K$ are convex and $F=H-K$ . Moreover, with $p(\mathbf{x})=\max\left\{\frac{L}{L_{F}}H(\mathbf{x}),\frac{L}{L_{F}}K(\mathbf{x})-\Delta\right\},\qquad q(\mathbf{x})=\frac{L}{L_{F}}K(\mathbf{x}),$ the functions $p,q$ are convex and satisfy $f=p-q$ . The displayed decomposition satisfies $\Lip(q)\leq L(N-1),\qquad\Lip(p)\leq LN.$

Remark C.2 (Comparison with the Kong–Lewis modulus) . Using the notation and DC comparison in Section 6 , the correction in Proposition C.1 gives $\Lambda(\delta)\leq M_{\rm DC}(f)\leq\Lip(q)\leq L(N-1).$ This is an upper bound only; it does not establish a lower bound proportional to $N$ for either intrinsic quantity. For $N\geq 2$ , the translation identity gives $K(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{u})=K(\mathbf{x})+(N-1)\alpha t$ for the maximum of the branch sums defining $K$ . The displayed correction $q=(L/L_{F})K$ therefore satisfies $q(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{u})-q(\mathbf{x})=\frac{L\alpha(N-1)}{L_{F}}t.$ Because $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1$ , this gives $\frac{L\alpha(N-1)}{L_{F}}\leq\Lip(q)\leq L(N-1).$ For the parameter choice in Lemma 4.1 , $\alpha/L_{F}>\epsilon/L$ . Thus, for $N\geq 2$ and a fixed ratio $\epsilon/L>0$ , the Lipschitz constant of this correction is bounded above and below by positive constants times $LN$ . These constants can depend on $\epsilon/L$ , but not on $d$ or $N$ . The lower bound concerns only the displayed correction and does not compare it with all other admissible corrections. Estimating $M_{\rm DC}(f)$ over all corrections, or estimating $\Lambda(\delta)$ , requires a separate argument.

Proposition D.1 (A two-branch function that is not weakly convex) . The interpolation formula ( 3.12 ), followed by the truncation ( 3.17 ), can define a function that is not $\varrho$ -weakly convex for any finite $\varrho\geq 0$ .
